claim: About one in four workers globally are in occupations with some GenAI exposure.
safe_wording: About one in four; exposure is potential exposure, not job loss.
caveat: Potential occupational exposure if technology is implemented; not actual adoption or displacement.

claim: 3.3% of global employment falls in the ILO's highest GenAI exposure category.
safe_wording: 3.3% is the highest exposure category, not a displacement forecast.
caveat: Exposure category does not mean all tasks or jobs will be automated.

claim: Employment with some GenAI exposure is estimated at 34% in high-income countries versus 11% in low-income countries.
safe_wording: Use as exposure contrast, not as 'risk' ranking.
caveat: Adoption constraints and labour-market composition differ by country.

claim: AI assistance increased customer-support productivity by 14% on average in a field study of 5,179 agents.
safe_wording: In this specific customer-support field study.
caveat: One occupational/company setting; do not generalise 14% to all work.

claim: In the same field study, productivity improved by 34% for novice and low-skilled workers, with minimal effects for experienced/high-skilled workers.
safe_wording: 34% for novice/low-skilled workers in this study.
caveat: Subgroup effect in one setting; mechanism is suggestive rather than universal.

claim: A Denmark study found no measurable average effect of AI-chatbot adoption on earnings or recorded hours within two years, ruling out effects larger than 2%.
safe_wording: No measurable average effect; the estimates rule out effects larger than 2%.
caveat: Null average effect does not mean no worker-level winners/losers or no task changes.

claim: PwC reports a 62% average wage premium for jobs requiring AI skills relative to comparable roles without those requirements.
safe_wording: PwC reports an average wage premium; treat as an observational job-ad association.
caveat: Not proof that acquiring an AI skill causes a 62% pay rise.

claim: PwC reports AI-skill job postings growing 69%, compared with 9% for the total jobs market in its analysis.
safe_wording: Within PwC's job-ad analysis.
caveat: Growth rates depend on PwC's definitions and dataset coverage.

claim: The most AI-exposed US entry-level roles were seven times more likely to demand traditionally senior human-intensive skills such as leadership and judgement.
population: 2.4 million US entry-level jobs in PwC analysis
safe_wording: Seven times more likely in PwC's US entry-level job-ad analysis.
caveat: Job-ad requirements are not the same as actual hiring decisions or worker capability.

claim: Employment of US workers aged 22–25 in highly AI-exposed occupations stood 19% below where it would have been if it had kept pace with less-exposed peers.
population: US workers aged 22–25 in ADP payroll data
safe_wording: A 19% relative employment gap; not a claim that AI caused all of it.
caveat: Observational labour-market pattern; researchers do not establish AI as the sole cause.

claim: OECD evidence says the broader deterioration in young people's labour-market outcomes began before the rise of current LLMs and does not currently show AI as the cause.
population: Young people across OECD labour markets
safe_wording: Use immediately beside the 19% Stanford finding.
caveat: Do not turn emerging AI-exposure patterns into a causal claim about youth unemployment.

claim: If the global workforce were 100 people, WEF estimates 59 would need training by 2030.
safe_wording: Employer-reported projection, not an observed outcome.
caveat: Future of Jobs projections cover multiple macrotrends, not AI alone.

claim: 63% of employers in the WEF survey identify skill gaps as a major barrier to business transformation.
safe_wording: 63% of surveyed employers.
caveat: Employer perceptions; not a worker survey.

claim: 77% of employers in the WEF survey plan to upskill workers in response to AI-related change.
safe_wording: 77% of surveyed employers plan to upskill workers.
caveat: Plans may not equal implementation.

claim: The IMF estimates about 26% of Indian workers are in occupations with high AI exposure: 14% in relatively complementary jobs and 12% in occupations at higher displacement risk.
safe_wording: Exposure framework: 14% complementary + 12% higher displacement risk.
caveat: Exposure/risk classification is not a forecast of actual jobs lost.

claim: NASSCOM expected India's AI talent pool to grow from roughly 600,000–650,000 to more than 1.25 million by 2027.
safe_wording: NASSCOM industry projection.
caveat: Industry projection; definition of AI talent and future growth assumptions matter.

claim: NASSCOM projected India's AI software/services market to grow at 25–35% CAGR through 2027.
safe_wording: Industry projection, 25–35% CAGR.
caveat: Market growth does not directly translate into employment growth.

claim: NASSCOM's 2026 Indian technology-industry research reports that 20–40% of work across participating technology organisations is being done through AI across functions.
population: Indian technology organisations in NASSCOM research
safe_wording: Indian technology-industry evidence only.
caveat: Do not generalise this to India's entire workforce.

claim: ILO Poland research found formal employer introduction of GenAI at 9.4%, while 16.7% of workers reported personal use in the previous week, suggesting adoption can outpace formal governance.
safe_wording: A Poland-specific workplace-adoption finding.
caveat: Country-specific; use as an organisational pattern, not a global rate.

claim: Experienced GenAI users in ILO focus groups tended to treat verification of AI output as a normal part of work; occasional users expressed more concern about creativity and erosion of core skills.
population: Workers/managers in ILO Poland qualitative research
safe_wording: Present as a qualitative theme, not a prevalence estimate.
caveat: Focus-group theme; do not attach a population percentage.

claim: Where GenAI was introduced with employee consultation, most surveyed workers used it and about two-thirds wanted to use it more; where dialogue was absent, 41% were firmly opposed.
safe_wording: Use to show organisational context matters.
caveat: Poland-specific; consultation is associated with attitudes, not proven as the sole cause.

claim: More than two-thirds of surveyed Polish workers reported receiving no guidance on workplace AI; only 2.1% reported clear prohibited-use boundaries.
safe_wording: Use as governance-gap evidence.
caveat: Country-specific.

claim: The supplied dataset contains 71,913 records covering 2020–2025.
safe_wording: The supplied dataset contains...
caveat: Dataset is not a representative sample of the global labour market.

claim: The overall median salary in the supplied dataset is $138,750; the middle 50% runs from $96,000 to $190,315.
safe_wording: Descriptive dataset statistic.
caveat: Heavy US and recent-year concentration.

claim: Median salary rises from $85,469 at entry level to $122,000 mid-level, $156,160 senior and $190,000 executive in the supplied dataset.
safe_wording: Raw medians by dataset experience label.
caveat: Not an estimate of the causal return to experience.

claim: In a 2024–2025 full-time adjusted model, AI/ML roles are associated with about 9.6% higher salary than classified software/engineering roles after controlling for experience, year, employee residence, work mode and company size.
safe_wording: Associated with about 9.6% higher salary after adjustment.
caveat: Observational association; omitted variables and dataset selection remain. Not a causal AI-skill premium.

claim: Only about 5.5% of records in the conservatively classified AI/ML archetype are entry-level; 63.2% are senior-level.
population: Conservatively classified AI/ML records in supplied dataset
safe_wording: Within this dataset's classified AI/ML records.
caveat: Does not prove AI reduced entry-level hiring; title mix and dataset construction can affect the distribution.

claim: 83.6% of dataset records list US employee residence, while only 0.3% list India.
safe_wording: Use as a limitation banner.
caveat: Do not use the project dataset to make representative claims about India.

claim: 91.7% of dataset records are from 2024–2025, so raw record-count growth over time should not be interpreted as job-market growth.
safe_wording: Use shares/composition rather than raw counts for temporal story claims.
caveat: Collection intensity differs sharply by year.
